soil-env-319.title: Shallow compaction of the plow layer
soil-env-319.text:
Shiny, cloddy furrows and deep ruts are the signs of shallow compaction, the compaction of the surface or plow layer found to some degree in all intensively worked agricultural soils. It results from lost aggregation, typically caused by erosion, low organic matter and the weight of field equipment. The first two cut the supply of sticky binding materials, and loosely bound soil is easier to press together, as in {{ref:soil-phys-001}}.

Moisture decides the damage. Soil wetter than its plastic limit is smeared into a dense mass by tillage or traffic, while friable soil below that limit crumbles and resists compaction. Sandy soils turn from plastic to friable quickly as they drain, whereas loams and clays need longer drying, and frozen soil is also resistant. The plastic limit belongs to {{ref:soil-phys-041}}.

Rain adds a second route. On unprotected soil it disperses wet aggregates into a thin dense layer that seals the surface and hardens into a crust. That cuts infiltration and can block seedling emergence, though residue cover and strong aggregation reduce it. Finally, a compacted soil tills up cloddy and needs extra secondary tillage and packing, which breaks aggregates and burns organic matter. Compaction therefore recurs in a vicious cycle.

soil-env-320.title: Subsoil compaction and the plow pan
soil-env-320.text:
Subsoil compaction is invisible unless you dig or push a rod into the soil. It is compaction deeper in the soil, often called a plow pan, though it has causes beyond plowing. It builds on the surface problem in {{ref:soil-env-319}}.

Subsoil compacts easily because it is usually wetter, denser, higher in clay, lower in organic matter and less aggregated than topsoil, and regular tillage does not loosen it. A surface load spreads through the soil in a cone, so pressure falls with depth. Light loads do little at depth, but heavy manure spreaders or combines compact deeply, and wet soil carries the force deeper. Plows and disks press down on the layer below, and tractor wheels in an open furrow press directly on the soil under the plow layer. Such pans may persist for many years after a field goes no-till.

Some soils are especially prone. Those with roughly equal sand, silt and clay and non-swelling 1:1 clays form dense subsoils when aggregates weaken from organic matter loss and silt and clay wash down into subsoil pores. Tropical oxisols with strongly aggregated clay can disperse when limed, because the raised pH lets clay particles wash into lower pores.

A ball test helps with timing. A handful from the lower plow layer that molds and sticks is too wet to work, while one that crumbles is dry enough for tillage or heavy traffic.

soil-phys-220.title: The non-limiting water range
soil-phys-220.text: Plants do not simply need water; they need water that is not locked behind hardness or drowned in poor air. The optimum water range for plant growth is the least-limiting water range. In a well-structured soil it runs from field capacity on the wet end to the wilting point on the dry end, the limits of {{ref:soil-water-229}}. In severely compacted soil the range is much narrower. At field capacity it is still too wet because it lacks large pores, and good aeration needs at least 20% of pore space air filled. On the dry end, growth in compacted soil is commonly limited by hardness rather than lack of available water. John Letey introduced the idea in 1985 to refine available water capacity. Da Silva, Kay and Perfect refined it in 1994 as the least limiting water range (LLWR).

soil-env-374.title: Assessing an urban site before sampling
soil-env-374.text:
The first step in assessing urban soil happens at a desk, not in the field: research the site's past use. Land-use history comes from owners, old aerial photos, maps, permits and tax records, plus a visit to look for sources such as peeling lead paint or a nearby highway. Green-space or residential histories usually mean fewer problems than industrial ones.

There are no federal contaminant limits in the US for gardens. The EPA recommends testing for pH, organic matter, nutrients, micronutrients and metals including lead. Samples may be needed per contaminant and at different depths, with metals near the surface and solvents deeper. Because distribution is unpredictable, many locations are needed, and suspect spots near old buildings, bare patches or drains need separate sampling. Lead rarely harms plants, but copper, zinc and nickel can be phytotoxic at high concentrations. A full assessment also considers slope, drainage and buried utility lines.

soil-env-373.title: Urban soil contamination and who it harms
soil-env-373.text:
Contamination is much more prevalent in urban soils than agricultural ones, and lead is the most common contaminant. Lead is widespread because of its long use in gasoline, banned in the US since 1989, and in paint, banned for residential use since 1978. Other contaminants include petroleum products and legacy pesticides such as lead arsenate and copper sulfate. Of special concern are former industrial sites, roadsides, recent construction sites, waste disposal sites and junkyards, and contaminants can also arrive by atmospheric deposition.

People are exposed by ingesting soil, breathing dust and volatiles, eating crops, and through skin. Risk is greatest on bare soil and for children. Plants absorb little lead, especially at neutral pH, so dirty hands, dust and unwashed produce are the larger exposure. Lead can accumulate in roots, so root crops should be avoided.

Other contaminants behave differently. Solvents such as trichloroethylene move readily to groundwater, some pesticides persist for years, and petroleum products tend to stay near the surface, where they can be scraped off. Road salt (sodium chloride) causes sodic conditions, aggregate breakdown and compaction.

soil-env-306.title: Urban soil: stripped, squeezed and contaminated
soil-env-306.text:
Under a city lawn or sidewalk, the soil is rarely the soil that was there before. Urban soil is soil in cities and towns, often stripped of its topsoil, compacted and contaminated by human activity. It holds more heavy metals, especially lead, copper and nickel, and has a lower pH than comparable soil in the wild. With the {{ref:soil-form-021}} typically stripped away, it has low aeration, porosity and drainage. Compaction, as in {{ref:soil-phys-082}}, and contamination limit root growth and tree health. Contamination persists in cities with a history of industry, leaded gasoline or lead-based house paint.

Construction rather than farm machinery is the usual cause of urban compaction. Jobs on tight schedules ignore the risk of working wet soil, and topsoil is stripped or fill added. Disturbed urban soils are low in organic matter and biological activity, and construction debris such as concrete often raises the pH because concrete contains lime.

The Polish soil classification's 'urban soils' type corresponds to Urbic, Mollic or Ecranic Technosols in the WRB. Management is interdisciplinary, aiming to protect soil biodiversity, cut industrial pollution and make soils more resilient to construction compaction. Recovery is possible: in a Palermo trial, de-sealing long-sealed urban soils and revegetating them stabilised infiltration and raised microbial activity within eighteen months.

soil-env-375.title: Reconditioning degraded urban soil
soil-env-375.text:
Reconditioning improves degraded {{ref:soil-env-306}} with physical, chemical and biological practices, generally applied in that order.

Physical work comes first. Removing contaminated soil by excavation is expensive and regulated. If contamination is modest or shallow, scraping the surface and replacing it with good topsoil is more feasible. Tillage or subsoiling can dilute a thin contaminated layer into deeper soil and relieve compaction, and where compaction is the main problem, amelioration in place is better than removal.

Chemical fixes follow. Phosphorus binds lead and makes it less dangerous over time, and lime or dolomite can stabilize pH. Biological and surface measures come last. Compost and other organic amendments raise organic matter, improve structure and biology, dilute toxic compounds and bind some contaminants, though the compost itself must be free of contaminants. Mulch suppresses weeds, reduces erosion and splash, and acts as a barrier to contact with contaminated soil.

soil-env-379.title: Protecting topsoil on a construction site
soil-env-379.text: Digging for pipes or drains mixes fertile topsoil with subsoil and leaves poor soil at the surface. Good construction practice limits traffic and protects topsoil to avoid lasting compaction and mixing of soil layers. Compaction, covered in {{ref:soil-phys-082}}, matters little under pavement but is a long-term problem where land is revegetated. Controlled traffic lanes, metal plates or geotextile under gravel, and avoiding work on wet soil limit it. The sequence is simple: strip and stockpile topsoil separately, refill subsoil first and loosen it with rippers, then replace topsoil without further compaction.

soil-env-377.title: Soil mixes for containers and green roofs
soil-env-377.text: A rooftop garden has a weight limit that a field never faces. Pots, planters and green roofs need clean, light soil mixes with excellent drainage and high water- and nutrient-holding capacity, quite unlike the natural textures of {{ref:soil-found-051}}. Rooftop mixes must be light enough not to overload the roof, yet heavy enough to anchor plants against wind and water. Mixes combine heat-treated vermiculite and perlite with organic materials such as peat moss, compost or biochar. They are low in density but cost more than ordinary soil.

soil-env-378.title: Gap-graded soil: pavement that lets roots breathe
soil-env-378.text: Street trees face a dilemma. Pavement needs a compacted substrate to bear loads, while roots need a healthy rooting environment, and trees often die early from constricted roots, salt, heat and moisture stress. Gap-graded soil answers it by containing only certain particle sizes, with some sizes left out deliberately to guarantee pore space. Large uniform stones form a load-bearing skeleton, while the large pores, partly filled with high-quality soil, let roots grow under the pavement. The pores are what compaction destroys in ordinary soil, as {{ref:soil-phys-082}} explains, and the mix departs from ordinary {{ref:soil-found-051}}. Golf greens use similar gap-graded sand to support foot traffic while keeping turf healthy.

soil-env-376.title: Remediating soil in urban green spaces
soil-env-376.text: Green spaces need soil with good drainage, high water-holding capacity and good rooting at low maintenance cost. Except in extreme contamination, poor soil can be buried under trucked-in topsoil or improved with amendments, as in {{ref:soil-env-375}}. Burying in place often suffices for built sites with debris. Raised beds or berms address poor soil and drainage, and landscape fabric under imported soil limits roots reaching the original soil. Two tools handle compaction. The scoop-and-dump method mixes compost into compacted soil with excavators, and an air spader blows compacted soil from around the roots of trees to be saved.

soil-env-372.title: The Food and Agriculture Organization
soil-env-372.text: The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) is a specialized agency that leads international efforts to defeat hunger and improve nutrition and food security. It was founded on 16 October 1945 in Quebec City and is headquartered in Rome. It has 194 members: 193 countries and the European Union. It helps coordinate improvements in agriculture, forestry, fisheries and land and water resources, giving technical assistance and collecting agricultural data. With the World Health Organization it created the Codex Alimentarius Commission in 1961 to develop food standards.

soil-env-326.title: Holistic management and the grazing debate
soil-env-326.text:
Holistic management is a systems-thinking approach to managing resources, first developed by Allan Savory for grazing management and now applied to other complex social, ecological and economic systems. It links to the whole-system thinking of {{ref:soil-env-218}}. Its decision framework tells managers to define the whole being managed, set goals, watch the earliest signs of ecosystem health such as bare ground, use any of eight tools, and test every decision. The tools include grazing, animal impact, fire and rest. Savory's principles hold that nature works as a community, that removing keystone species such as large herds has wide effects, that livestock can substitute for lost herds, and that timing is the key factor in land use.

The evidence is disputed, and peer-reviewed studies disagree on whether planned grazing outperforms continuous grazing or sequesters carbon at the rates its founder claimed. A 1972-2016 meta-analysis and a 2022 review of 22 farm-scale studies found no productivity gain, while defenders say trials miss its goal setting and monitoring, and some studies show soil gains. A 2016 Swedish study put the real carbon sequestration rate of improved grazing management at seven times lower than Savory's claims. One 2011 study found multi-paddock grazing stored slightly less soil carbon than excluding livestock.

soil-env-332.title: What a healthy soil looks like
soil-env-332.text:
Farmers say soil health and scientists say soil quality, and both mean how well a soil functions for the use being considered, as in {{ref:soil-env-179}}. Soil health stresses the human influence of years of intensive management, as distinct from inherent differences from parent material and climate, much as a person's health depends on how the body is treated.

Farmers recognize good soil by its dark, crumbly look, higher yields for less effort, less runoff and erosion, and the lower power needed to run machinery than on compacted soil. A healthy soil has enough nutrients all season, good {{ref:soil-phys-039}}, stable structure that aids infiltration and water storage ({{ref:soil-phys-004}}), and enough depth before a compact layer or bedrock. It drains well enough for timely field work and lets oxygen in and carbon dioxide out of the root zone, with exceptions such as flooded soils for cranberries and paddy rice.

It has low disease, parasite and weed pressure, many beneficial organisms such as earthworms, bacteria and fungi, and no harmful chemicals, whether natural, like soluble aluminum or excess salts, or human-made, like fuel oil or toxic sludge. A high-quality soil also resists degradation and is resilient, recovering quickly after unfavorable changes such as compaction.
